answers.question: I haven't run for two weeks. Do I have to start again from the beginning? And is the 5K in four weeks still realistic?
answers.answer:
**You do not need to start again from the beginning.** Two weeks off costs you a little, not the work you put in before. This week begins one step below your last sessions, and by Wednesday you are back to 8 x 2 min run and 1 min walk.

**The race is still worth running, but running the whole 5 km without a walk is now a stretch.** Your longest unbroken run is 2 minutes, and a 5K at a comfortable pace takes roughly 40 to 45 minutes. You have this week, two more build weeks and then race week.

This is the rough direction for the run blocks if the sessions keep feeling easy. I will adjust it to how each week goes.

| Week | Longest run block | Running time per session |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oct 19 – 25 | 3 min | 14 – 18 min |
| Oct 26 – Nov 1 | 5 min | about 20 min |
| Nov 2 – 8 | 8 to 10 min | about 24 min |
| Nov 9 – 15 | race week | the 5K on Sun Nov 15 |

By the week of Nov 2 – 8 we will know whether the whole way is realistic. If it is not, you can still finish your first 5K, running most of it with a few walk breaks planned in advance.

new.analysis:
Two weeks away has cost you very little fitness, so this week is a gentle re-entry rather than a restart. You missed all three planned sessions in the week of Oct 12 – 18 and ran none the week before, which fits what was happening with your mum. I'm glad she is home. After a gap this short, the first run or two usually feel heavier than they are, and that passes quickly.

The peak label does not mean speed work for you. In a normal peak phase I would add running at race pace, but you are building toward running continuously. For you, the race-specific work is longer unbroken blocks at an easy effort. Everything this week is easy, because adding harder running now would raise your injury risk for almost no gain.

The week is built so two runs bring you back and the third moves you forward. The third run changes block length, not total running time, so the step is smaller than it looks. That keeps the jump manageable after a fortnight off.

Pace matters as much as block length. On Sat Oct 3 your run blocks were around 7:40/km, and almost the whole session sat in heart-rate zone 3, averaging 143 beats per minute (about 79 percent of your max). That is fine for 2-minute blocks but too quick to hold for 10 minutes or more. Running slower now is what makes longer blocks possible.

For the race itself, I will look at how Saturday and the following week go, then set your race-day plan. If you are not running the whole way by the week of Nov 2 – 8, I would rather you plan walk breaks at set times than walk only when you are out of breath. That keeps the finish feeling strong, and a whole-way 5K can be the aim for your next race. Race week will be lighter, with fewer minutes and nothing new.

With about six hours of sleep and high stress, the plan can bend. If a morning falls through, do not make it up, just carry on with the next session. If you miss two sessions in one week, repeat that week's level instead of moving on.
